units.translation: For shame, being in the assemblies (thus Bamberger for λεχθεῖσιν [the things said]), makes words blind.
a white spot on the eye
i.e. it will be of no help to him.
Which of the gods or goddesses will come to my aid?
For these things will not help him at all to avoid falling in dishonor, a fall not to be endured.
And no remedy helped (thus Blomfield for ἐπήρκεσαν [they helped]) to prevent the city from suffering as it now does.
Thus corrected from the copy, which has Μἄπαρχός [commander] with a double accent.

Thus here too Canterus for ἄπαρχος [first-fruit offering]. The third example is Ch. 664, where in M is written γυνή τάπαρχος [the woman the commander], but with a superscript o, by which τόπαρχος [the local commander] is indicated, whether by the first hand or by the διορθωτή [corrector]. In that place neither γυνή τ᾽ ἔπαρχος [and the woman the commander] can be written nor what Ahrens conjectured in Philologus Supplement vol. 1 p. 629, γυνή γ᾽ ἄπαρχος [the woman indeed the first-fruit offering], can be approved. Bamberger conjectured στέγαρχος [master of the house].
And commander of the ships and destroyer of Ilium.
the woman indeed the first-fruit offering

The scholiast explains: ἀλλεπάλληλον κτύπον ποιοῦντα [making a repeated din]. The Homeric ἐπασσύτεροι [one after another], on which see Thes. vol. 3 p. 1439, Hesychius explains by ἄλλοι ἐπ᾿ ἄλλοις [one after another].
The frequent blows of the hand's reach.
to enjoy, to reap benefit and fruit
I enjoy, I reap benefit and fruit. The aorist of the middle form is ἐπηυρόμην [I enjoyed].

where M has ἐπηύρω [I enjoyed], some copies have ἀπ ἀπηύρω [I enjoyed from]. Elmsley rightly reads ἐπηύρου [you enjoyed]: for the ancients said ἐπαυρέσθαι [to enjoy], not ἐπαύρασθαι [to enjoy]: on which see Thes. vol. 3 p. 1443.
Such things you enjoyed from your kindly disposition.
to shout in response, in an obscure and corrupt passage
I shout in response, in an obscure and corrupt passage
Having shouted in response to your father's deed.
in a verse invented by an interpolator to fill a lacuna.
Touching with fearless hand and merely grasping.
From the touch and inspiration of Zeus.
Epaphus, son of Io by Zeus
Epaphus, son of Io by Zeus
Epaphus truly named from the laying on of hands.
Speaking of this race, you would hit upon Epaphus.
to pour in addition; improperly, to mix in
I pour in addition; improperly, I mix in

in the words of Clytaemnestra to the chorus. For thus it is corrected from what is read in M: θροῶ ἐπεγχέασα [I cry out, pouring in], which the scholiast explains as συναναμίξασα [mixing together]. Yet this use of the verb is strange and suspect.
For you cry out my suffering, pouring it in.
It has the meaning of time from which, as ἀφ᾽ οὗ [from which].
serving to give a reason, it can be rendered in Latin in various ways: since, inasmuch as, because.
